item.title: Moving Beyond Wellness to Empowerment
item.description:
Health

Moving Beyond Wellness to Empowerment

Successful wellness programs may depend upon empowering, not just educating.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Though intuitively compelling, resilience and wellness programs have proven disappointing.
  • Poor compliance appears to be problematic.
  • Shifting from wellness to empowerment programs may improve compliance.
  • Integrating two powerful public health strategies may improve compliance and overall effectiveness.
Source: DGSstudios / Pixabay

No matter what the occupation, talent is at the center of it. Anything that threatens the well-being of the worker threatens the viability of the mission and thus the viability of the organization itself. Conversely, anything that promotes the well-being of the worker enhances the viability of the mission and thus the viability of the organization itself. Health resides at the center of personal and organizational viability; thus, the desire to promote health using workplace-based platforms should be no surprise. The workplace is where most people spend a significant proportion of their waking adult life. The implementation of resilience and wellness programs at the workplace would seem to be a compelling approach to fostering health.

Effectiveness of Resilience and Wellness Programs

Within the field of occupational health promotion, resilience programs and workplace-based wellness programs have grown meteorically in popularity within the last 15 years. That said, the overall effectiveness of resilience programs has been disappointing (Eidelson et al., 2011; Fikretoglu et al., 2019), while the effectiveness of occupational wellness programs appears to be modest at best (Virtanen et al., 2025).

While the reasons for the disappointing outcomes associated with resilience and wellness programs are varied and multifactorial, the primary reason appears to be the inability to sustain compliance. Putative reasons for poor compliance include: programs being constructed on a fundamentally flawed negative reinforcement paradigm that requires delayed gratification; failure to elevate resilience and wellness to a cultural expectation; failure to mobilize systemic support for success. Most fundamentally, however, Virginia Satir may have most concisely explained the psychological resistance to self-improvement: People prefer the certainty of misery to the misery of uncertainty (fear of the unknown).

Empower, Don’t Compensate

Resilience programs, and to some degree wellness programs, are often perceived as compensatory, which implies weakness, injury, or disease. They often involve ambiguous “psychological” methods. At the very least, they promote change and therefore uncertainty. The notion of making strong people stronger through a predictable empowerment approach may resonate more constructively.

There are two evidence-based approaches to empowerment worthy of mention in the present context: 1) Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), and 2) Bandura’s self-efficacy.

The Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM; Witte, 1992) is a powerful heuristic which was originally used to explain how people respond to fear-based messaging, especially public health messaging. But it provides us with important insight into why resilience and wellness programs succeed or fail. The model explains that there are three essential steps required for people to take action toward self-improvement and empowerment: 1) severity (there is a problem or at least sufficient rationale for change), 2) susceptibility (the problem or rationale is personally relevant), and 3) control (there is a high likelihood of successful change engendered by a sense of personal control).

Simple motivation, however, may not be enough to increase and sustain compliance with behavior change programs. The missing element may be self-efficacy (Bandura, 1997). Self-efficacy may be thought of as the belief in one’s own ability to exercise reasonable control over one’s life. Bandura believed self‑efficacy is the central mechanism of human resilience, well-being, and successful adaptation. He noted people who believe they have the power to exercise some measure of control over their lives are healthier, more effective, and more successful.

So, the question is: How can self-efficacy be increased? Fortunately, Bandura has provided a simple yet effective teaching framework that can serve as the superstructure for resilience and wellness programs:

  1. Observation sets the foundation for success. Provide relevant role models who can demonstrate the resilience and wellness behaviors required for successful outcomes. Ideally, they manifest the desired changes themselves as well.
  2. Success begets success. Provide opportunities to experience success applying the principles and actions required for resilience and wellness. Start small using successive approximation.
  3. Provide catalysts for success. Provide the opportunity for coaching, mentoring, and peer support.
  4. Provide instruction in and reinforcement for self-control and managing stress. Stress management aspects of resilience and wellness programs appear to be the most successful.

The core assertion of this missive is that in order for resilience and wellness programs to meet their full potential, they must incorporate evidence-based strategies for behavior change: 1) EPPM and 2) self-efficacy.

item.title: Clinical Wisdom: More Secrets of the Therapeutic Alliance
item.description:
Therapy

Clinical Wisdom: More Secrets of the Therapeutic Alliance

What is therapist transparency and how important is it?

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Therapist transparency exists on a broad spectrum depending upon the practitioner and theoretical orientation.
  • Too much transparency can diminish the healing power of therapy.
  • There is some middle ground between therapeutic transparency and abstinence.

This is Part 8 of a series.

In Part 7 of this series on clinical wisdom, I discussed the so-called therapeutic alliance and its scientifically proven powerful role in psychotherapy. Here, we continue that conversation.

Freud's famous psychoanalytic couch
Source: JRennocks/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 4.0

Therapist Transparency: To Share or Not to Share?

Psychotherapy, in actuality, is traditionally a unique kind of interpersonal and intimate relationship in which the therapist gets to know the client or patient (or, at least, as much as they are willing to reveal about themselves) while the patient typically knows almost nothing about the personal life of the therapist (beyond what can be gleaned indirectly in conversation and observation). Such relative anonymity on the part of the therapist, much like an enigmatic Rorschach inkblot, invites and promotes projection of the patient's unconscious conflicts, feelings, and concerns. It is an extraordinarily one-sided relationship in this regard, but this is fitting because psychotherapy is all about the patient and their lives, concerns, and problems, not the therapist's. Indeed, this lack of mutuality as regards self-revelation is what differentiates and distinguishes therapy from friendship and other types of human relationships. It could be argued that without the intentional practice of anonymity by the clinician, therapy is diluted and reduced to something akin to a formalized friendship. But friendship is not therapy and therapy is not friendship, though there may be elements of each in both.

Of course, this imbalanced stance can be uncomfortable for patients, in part because the last thing they want to do is to make themselves emotionally vulnerable in the presence of some stranger, expert, or authority figure. But doing so is what psychotherapy is fundamentally all about: Humbly confessing one's confusion, frustration, fear, or abject inability or powerlessness to resolve the distressing presenting symptom or problematic situation. Bravely baring one's soul to another, albeit unknown, human being and, in the process of so doing, simultaneously to oneself. For most of us, this can be quite hard on the ego, which is why entering therapy tends for most people, especially men, to be difficult and anxiety-provoking, and often engenders strong resistance. In Jungian terms, we might say that the narcissistic or grandiose ego, which strives to be in complete control, must sacrifice or mortify itself in service of the Self, and that mustering the courage to enter psychotherapy is the auspicious start of this labyrinthine "individuation" process toward wholeness, balance, integrity, and authenticity. (See my prior post.)

Some contemporary clinicians, such as Yalom (1991) and a number of other humanistic and existential therapists, for instance, have come to the conclusion that deliberately being vulnerable themselves in therapy, being completely open or "transparent" with their patients or clients about themselves, promotes, models, and encourages the person's willingness to reciprocally reveal themselves in the therapy relationship. And it may in fact have this effect with certain patients. Indeed, for practitioners like Yalom, it has become their intrinsic go-to style of psychotherapy, to which they attribute its perceived success or efficacy.

But is such therapist transparency really necessary, more efficacious, and truly in the client's or patient's best interest? Is therapist transparency the only and best way to deepen and fortify the therapeutic alliance? Or, could it conceivably have the opposite effect of diluting, watering down, and diminishing the inherent power of psychotherapy? Might it be possible that the psychotherapist's humanity, empathy, genuineness, and vulnerability is better communicated and demonstrated not by breaking the boundary or rule of abstinence first recommended by Freud (1914/1915), but rather by their consistent and caring presence, receptivity, curiosity, and commitment to the here-and-now encounter with what the person is saying or not saying, doing or not doing, feeling or not feeling in the moment. Could a psychotherapist's intentionally revealing personal things about themselves be seen by cynics as a subtly manipulative though well-intentioned technique, trick, or method to get the patient to more quickly confide in the clinician by responding in kind?

Therapeutic Abstinence

For Freud, psychoanalytic abstinence was a basic clinical principle adhered to by the analyst partly to avoid gratifying or indulging the patient's crucial transferential fantasies of receiving parental love, attention, and affection, friendship, or romantic love from the clinician. Yes, the patient desires and deserves to have these normal human needs met in their lives, but the psychodynamic psychotherapist knows that gratifying these fantasies within the therapy relationship can detract from the person's motivation to seek their appropriate fulfillment outside of and beyond therapy (i.e., after termination) and their willingness to look within themselves for an understanding of what has thus far been preventing this to happen in their lives during therapy.

The role of the therapist is not to become their father, mother, best friend, or lover (despite the patient projecting this upon us to some extent) but to help the patient to consciously recognize that they have been unconsciously acting out their unmet dependency needs, acknowledge the futility of this behavior, and accept responsibility for their own role in finding (or not finding) friendship, support, and love in the world right now and in the future. It is, in some ways, the frustration (and sometimes anger) felt by the patient in response to the therapist's abstinence, withholding, and emotional unavailability that ultimately motivates them to pursue these needs outside of therapy and to create more of the kind of life they envision for themselves. This is the quintessential secret power of psychotherapy.

Certainly, some self-disclosure on the clinician's part can be helpful in cultivating and maintaining the therapeutic alliance—as, for instance, in dealing with the phenomenon of countertransference and particularly projective identification or selectively sharing a personal or professional experience relevant to that which the patient is presently struggling—but it is best engaged in sparingly and only for good reasons rather than rotely, regularly, or routinely. Any more than this runs the risk of radically reducing the essential power and depth of the transformative alchemical psychotherapy process, which depends partially upon the projection of the patient's unconscious onto the clinician and its careful and collaborative acknowledgment and analysis. In any case, this begs the clinical question: While the quality of the relationship between patient and therapist is clearly central to the therapy project, however this is accomplished or consciously promoted by the clinician, is the mere presence of a positive therapeutic alliance in and of itself a sufficient condition for successful psychotherapy? Carl Rogers (1951) believed so, but this seems to me a somewhat simplistic and naive view of how psychotherapy really works, as we shall explore further in the next post in this series.

item.title: How to Deal With Bullsh*t
item.description:
Illusory Truth Effect

How to Deal With Bullsh*t

Why truth-indifference works, and how to stop helping it spread.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Repetition can make claims feel truer even when no new evidence appears.
  • Bullsh*t may persuade better than lying because truth-indifference is harder to detect.
  • Good-enough approximations stay adaptive only while they remain open to correction.
  • Responding well means naming the tactic without feeding the outrage that spreads it.
A microphone can amplify a claim without making it true.
Source: Srattha Nualsate / Pexels

We know the feeling before words present themselves, as our BS detectors are visceral. Someone says something—in a meeting, in a comment thread—and you just know. It may not be a lie; a lie would at least offer something to disprove. This is slipperier. You cannot tell whether the person believes it, means it, or knows what he is doing. I can't tell if he's doing it on purpose. Not-knowing is the fulcrum, more particularly knowing there is a not-knowing brewing. In the meantime, BS is working on less conscious levels, already.

Why Bullsh*t Can Beat Lying

New research puts flesh on the bones. Petrocelli and colleagues asked participants to judge claims attributed to an ordinary person, a liar, or a bullsh*tter. The bullsh*tter was treated no worse than the ordinary person and as more believable than the liar. Repeated claims attributed to the bullsh*tter also produced a pronounced illusory-truth effect: familiarity made them feel more true, even when repetition added no evidence (Petrocelli et al., 2026).

That result sits inside a much larger literature. A recent meta-analysis of 182 studies, including more than 31,000 participants, confirmed that repetition produces a small but robust increase in perceived truth (Ye et al., 2026). We are not simply evaluating content. We are also registering ease, familiarity, confidence, and the social presentation of the person speaking.

In On Bullsh*t, Frankfurt distinguished lying from bullsh*t by the speaker's relationship to truth (Frankfurt, 2005). A liar must track reality closely enough to conceal it. A bullsh*tter need not: The statement may be true, false, mixed, or impossible to evaluate. What has dropped out is a commitment to finding out which. From the outside, both may perform sincerity. My practical extension of Frankfurt is this: The difference begins to show when reality pushes back. Can the claim be tested, corrected, or revised?

Bullsh*t Is Part of the Operating System

I have argued the uncomfortable half of this before: A nervous system exists to “approximate whatever is external at least well enough to survive.” The amount of information available far exceeds the bandwidth and channels available. We live by models, not by direct possession of the world, and most of those models have to be good enough before they can be exact. This is adaptive epistemic ambiguity, not a defect in need of eradication (Brenner, 2025b).

BS is essentially a core part of the human operating system. It remains adaptive when the approximation is connected to feedback, consequences, and revision. It becomes insidious when that corrective wire is cut—when evidence no longer changes the story, contradiction becomes somebody else's problem, and the appearance of sincerity substitutes for accountability.

BRODA Up Close

I have called one version of this BRODA: Bait, Refuse Open Dialogue, and Attack (Brenner, 2025a). They always start with bullsh*t. A question appears to invite an answer, but no answer can alter the exchange. Dialogue closes, the target keeps trying to restore it, and the roles turn over: The person asking for reality-testing is recast as hostile, unstable, or unfair.

The perpetrator is often unaware of it. That is one reason trying to read motive can become its own trap. There may be no fully formed plan to uncover, only a process unfolding through the interaction. You do not have to prove intention in order to respond. Ask what evidence supports the claim, what would count against it, and whether the speaker is willing to be corrected. If those questions are refused and the exchange turns personal, the refusal is information.

The Outrage Trap

This is where the wish for fairness becomes vulnerability. Research on belief in a just world shows how deeply people need to experience events as orderly and morally intelligible (Lerner & Simmons, 1966; Lerner, 1980). Bad-faith messaging recruits “a sense of righteous indignation, a desire for a ‘just world’... which drives engagement on the side of the recipient of the objectionable messaging.”

Correction can enter the same machinery. In a large study of replies to misleading posts on X, the appearance of community fact-checks increased negativity, anger, disgust, and moral outrage in the replies (Chuai et al., 2025). That does not mean correction is useless. It means correction may also intensify the engagement surrounding the original claim.

The practical move is more subtle than either silence or verbal jousting or debate. Correct the claim for the bystanders and witnesses. State plainly the evidence. Name the refusal to engage, without pretending to know what is in the other person's mind. Do not stay for the prolonged performance once it becomes clear that correction has no place to land. Unless you are a master communicator, discretion is the better part of valor, as the usual attempts to rebut only add fuel to the fire.

Truth Is a Practice

Dealing with bullsh*t does not require purity, and it does not require certainty about intention. It asks whether a claim remains in relationship with evidence, whether correction is possible, and whether continuing the exchange serves understanding or merely feeds the cycle.

The higher-order idea of Truth: a human accomplishment, something people keep making through attention, disagreement, revision, and the willingness to discover that a good-enough story is no longer good enough.

We are often manifestations of the very processes about which we are most curious.
